claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution in high-entropy nanoalloys.
High configurational entropy and nanoscale grains act synergistically to suppress elemental segregation.
High configurational entropy and nanoscale grains suppress nucleation of deleterious phases.
The proposed entropy–grain-size synergy suppresses formation of non-protective oxides.
The entropy–grain-size synergy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
A refined grain structure minimizes sites for localized oxidation.
Refractory and multi-principal-element alloys are relevant candidates for high-temperature applications.

Laser powder-bed fusion can produce the refractory W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 high-entropy alloy with complete fusion and without a significant number of undissolved particles when favorable process parameters are used.
The cited laser-based process produces a uniformly mixed nanocrystalline alloy.
Nanoscale grain boundaries and the interfacial-energy landscape influence diffusion.
Nanoscale grain boundaries and the interfacial-energy landscape influence elemental segregation.
A finer grain structure distributes potential reactive sites more uniformly.
A finer grain structure promotes formation of a coherent, self-healing protective oxide or minimizes deleterious oxide growth.
A finer grain structure limits local chemical fluctuations.
Nanocrystalline samples will retain a single-phase solid solution better than coarse-grained samples of the same composition after high-temperature exposure.
Nanocrystalline samples will exhibit less elemental segregation than coarse-grained samples after high-temperature exposure.
Nanocrystalline samples will have lower oxidation rates and lower weight gain than coarse-grained samples because their oxide is more protective.
Coarse-grained or partially homogenized high-entropy alloys are more prone to local segregation and phase decomposition during high-temperature annealing.
Processing defects or compositional inhomogeneities can dominate the proposed stabilizing effects and cause deviation from the prediction.
The prediction may fail when the oxide is not self-limiting.
